## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization of the per-particle update can approach the streaming ceiling on this workload.

## Cache saturation
All measured N (4000–4M) exceed the L1d spill (N≈949). At q=0.01, cost FALLS from 8.753 ns/p (N=4000) to 8.081 (N=16000) — overhead amortization — then stays FLAT at ~8.0 through the L2→DRAM spill (N≈60787, between N=16000 and N=65000) with no knee. At q=0.05 the shape repeats: 11.732 falls to 8.356, flat at ~8.3, then rises to 8.83 at N≥1M. At q=0.25, 13.395 falls to 9.85 and flattens at ~10.2. Death rate raises the floor (8.0→8.3→10.2 ns/p) without changing the N-shape: no cache-spill knee at any q.

## Bandwidth
Peak is 8.67 GB/s at N=262000, q=0.01 — 34% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling. The algo is compute/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Performance is stable across N within each death rate but degrades with churn: q=0.01 sustains ~8.6 GB/s (34%), q=0.05 ~8.3 GB/s (33%) dropping to 7.81 (31%) at N≥1M, and q=0.25 falls to 6.74 GB/s (27%). The transition is driven by death rate, not by N or cache spill.

## Assembly
The compiler did not vectorize the particle update. The inner loop uses scalar `s`-registers only: `ldp s5, s6`, `ldp s7, s16`, `ldr s17`, `fadd s5`, `fmul s5`, `fcvtzs`, `fcmp`, `csel` — one particle at a time. The histogram reports 0 vector-suffixed instructions. The only SIMD is a death-scan pre-pass (`ldp q1, q0`, `orr.16b`, `ext.16b`, `orr.8b`) OR-reducing 32 flags. The scatter writeback is byte-granular: 45 `ldrb` and 16 `strb` with `csel` saturation clamps, plus 37 `bl` calls to `spawn`. Scalar FP plus byte-level load-modify-store explains the 34% ceiling fraction.

## Verdict
Refuted — the compiler emitted no vectorized particle-update code (0 vector-suffixed instructions; all scalar `s`-register ops), and peak bandwidth is 8.67 GB/s = 34% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling. The byte-granular scatter (45 `ldrb`/16 `strb`) and 37 `bl` respawn calls cap performance regardless of death rate, confirming auto-vectorization cannot approach the streaming ceiling here.
